title: From Intent to Action: Benchmarking LLM Safety in Vehicle Voice Command Authorization
content:
Computer Science > Artificial Intelligence
  [Submitted on 17 Sep 2026]
    Title:From Intent to Action: Benchmarking LLM Safety in Vehicle Voice Command Authorization
View PDF HTML (experimental)
            Abstract:Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly integrated into vehicle voice assistants. But linking natural-language requests to vehicle functions creates a safety-critical authorization problem. Before executing a command, the system must choose whether to execute, refuse, clarify, require confirmation, defer to manual control, trigger an emergency response, or make no tool call. To our knowledge, prior evaluations do not isolate this pre-action decision across speaker role, authentication status, vehicle state, and tool availability. We introduce a 202-scenario benchmark with Reference Decisions under a seven-class taxonomy. We evaluate two local open-weight models and three API-based LLMs using Decision Alignment and safety-specific error metrics. Alignment ranges from 40.1% for Llama 3.2 3B to 89.1% for Gemini 3.1 Pro Preview. The API-based models score between 83.2% and 89.1%, with no statistically significant differences among them. Even these models produce two to three False Executes among 161 non-execution scenarios, and persistent errors remain in confirmation and manual-control decisions. A controlled Llama 3.2 3B ablation increases alignment to 40.1% under the structured authorization policy, versus 28.2-29.2% under schema-only and generic-safety baselines, but it does not eliminate False Executes. Structured LLM decisions are therefore insufficient as a standalone safety mechanism, and deployment requires an independent enforcement layer that verifies tool permissions and vehicle-state constraints before invoking any vehicle function.

report.summary: A new 202-scenario benchmark finds even top LLMs misauthorize vehicle voice commands, with false executes persisting, so structured decisions alone are unsafe.
report.background: Large language models are moving into vehicle voice assistants, letting drivers use natural language to control navigation, climate, windows, and other functions. That creates a safety-critical authorization problem: before executing a request, the system must decide whether to execute, refuse, clarify, require confirmation, defer to manual control, trigger emergency response, or make no tool call. Prior evaluations have not isolated this pre-action decision across speaker role, authentication status, vehicle state, and tool availability. This paper introduces a 202-scenario benchmark with Reference Decisions and a seven-class taxonomy, then evaluates local open-weight and API-based LLMs using Decision Alignment and safety-specific error metrics. It also tests whether structured authorization policies improve performance without eliminating dangerous false executions.
key_points: The paper introduces a 202-scenario benchmark with a seven-class Reference Decision taxonomy: execute, refuse, clarify, require confirmation, defer to manual control, trigger emergency response, or make no tool call. It isolates the pre-action authorization decision across speaker role, authentication status, vehicle state, and tool availability—variables that prior safety evaluations largely overlooked in vehicle voice assistants.

Decision Alignment varies sharply by model: Llama 3.2 3B reaches 40.1%, while Gemini 3.1 Pro Preview reaches 89.1%. Three API-based LLMs score 83.2% to 89.1%, with no statistically significant differences among them. This suggests scale and API access improve authorization decisions, but even leading models remain imperfect.

Safety-specific error metrics reveal that the best API models still produce two to three False Executes across 161 non-execution scenarios. Errors persist especially in confirmation and manual-control decisions. False Executes are dangerous because a wrong tool call can directly actuate vehicle functions, so high average alignment does not guarantee safe operation.

A controlled Llama 3.2 3B ablation shows a structured authorization policy raises alignment to 40.1%, versus 28.2–29.2% under schema-only and generic-safety baselines. However, the policy does not eliminate False Executes. The authors conclude structured LLM decisions are insufficient as a standalone safety mechanism and must be paired with independent enforcement.

The recommended architecture treats the LLM as an intent interpreter, not the final authority. Deployment requires an independent enforcement layer that verifies tool permissions and vehicle-state constraints before invoking any vehicle function. This separation is critical for safety-critical domains where natural-language ambiguity, authentication context, and dynamic vehicle states can turn a plausible command into an unsafe action.
report.impact: For the AI industry, the study reinforces that agentic LLMs cannot be trusted as final safety authorities in physical systems. It pushes automakers and AI vendors toward layered architectures: LLM intent parsing plus deterministic policy enforcement, permission checks, and vehicle-state validation. Developers should benchmark pre-action decisions, not just language quality; they must track false executes, confirmation behavior, and manual-control fallbacks. For regular users, voice assistants may still mishear or misauthorize commands, so confirmation prompts and manual overrides remain essential. The finding may slow deployment of fully autonomous voice control while accelerating standards for safety guardrails in vehicles and other cyber-physical AI systems.
report.tools: Follow the arXiv paper’s benchmark design and metrics. For implementation, watch NVIDIA NeMo Guardrails and Guardrails AI for policy-based LLM enforcement; Open Policy Agent for external authorization; COVESA Vehicle Signal Specification (VSS) for vehicle-state constraints; and AUTOSAR Adaptive or ROS 2 for safe vehicle integration. These tools help build the independent enforcement layer the paper calls for rather than relying on model alignment alone.
